sections.title: Start here
sections.body:
Soil is grains, water and air. Geotechnical questions start by describing that mixture, then ask how much load it can carry and how it will settle or push on a wall.

The idea behind most of the topic is effective stress: the grains carry only the part of the load that the water does not.
pitfalls: Using total stress where effective stress is needed below the water table.
Confusing void ratio (voids over solids) with porosity (voids over total volume).

items: The coefficients of uniformity and curvature are quick formula lookups. Expect them.
For phase relations go back to the definitions and a phase diagram: weight of water over weight of solids, volume of voids over volume of solids.
A specification such as 95% of standard Proctor means relative compaction: field dry density over the laboratory maximum. Fill is placed in lifts so that each one can be compacted.
Be careful interpolating on charts with a logarithmic axis; a straight-line estimate by eye can be well off.
Bearing capacity is substitution once the factors are known. Check the units of each term.

bridge.plain: Geotechnical engineering treats soil as a building material. Soil is grains with water and air in the gaps, and its strength comes from the grains pressing and rubbing on each other.
core: Describe a soil by how much of it is solid, water and air.
Water in the gaps carries part of the load; only the rest (effective stress) gives the soil strength.
Clay squeezes slowly under load, which causes settlement.
Strength is friction plus cohesion; it governs walls, footings and slopes.
bridge.links: It uses water pressure from fluids, stress and Mohr's circle from mechanics of materials, and force balance from statics. Pavement subgrades link it to transportation.

sections.title: Index properties and soil classifications
sections.body:
Index properties are quick measurements that tell soils apart. Grain size distribution, from sieving, shows whether a soil is gravel, sand or fines. The coefficients of uniformity and curvature say whether the sizes are well mixed.

For fine soils, the Atterberg limits mark the water contents at which the soil changes behaviour: the plastic limit (crumbly to mouldable) and the liquid limit (mouldable to runny). Their difference is the plasticity index. The Unified system (USCS) gives two-letter symbols such as SW, CL and GP. The AASHTO system rates soils for use as road subgrade.
pitfalls: Mixing up D_{10} and D_{60}: D_{10} is the finer size.
Taking the plastic limit for the plasticity index. PI is the liquid limit minus the plastic limit.

example.problem: A soil has D_{10} = 0.1 mm, D_{30} = 0.3 mm and D_{60} = 0.9 mm. Find C_{u} and C_{c}.

ideas.title: Dual symbols
ideas.text: A coarse-grained soil with 5% to 12% fines gets a dual symbol, such as SW-SM, that reports both its grading and the plasticity of its fines.

ideas.title: Well graded or uniform
ideas.text: A well-graded soil has many sizes, so small grains fill the gaps between large ones and its gradation curve is long and smooth. A uniform soil is mostly one size, like beach sand, and its curve is steep. The No. 200 sieve, 0.075 mm, separates sand from fines.

ideas.title: Plasticity index
ideas.text: The plasticity index is the range of water content over which the soil behaves plastically: PI = LL - PL. With the liquid limit it places a fine-grained soil on the plasticity chart for classification.

ideas.title: Coefficient of uniformity
ideas.text: The coefficient of uniformity, C_{u} = D_{60} / D_{10}, measures the spread of particle sizes. The coefficient of curvature, C_{c} = D_{30}^{2} / (D_{60} × D_{10}), measures the shape of the curve. Both are needed to call a sand or gravel well graded.

examples.problem: A clay has a liquid limit of 48 and a plastic limit of 21. What is its plasticity index?
examples.idea: The plasticity index is the range of water content over which the soil behaves plastically: PI = LL - PL. With the liquid limit it places a fine-grained soil on the plasticity chart for classification.

examples.problem: A grain size curve gives D_{60} = 1.8 mm, D_{30} = 0.6 mm and D_{10} = 0.15 mm. What is the coefficient of uniformity?
examples.idea: The coefficient of uniformity, C_{u} = D_{60} / D_{10}, measures the spread of particle sizes. The coefficient of curvature, C_{c} = D_{30}^{2} / (D_{60} × D_{10}), measures the shape of the curve. Both are needed to call a sand or gravel well graded.

examples.problem: A clay has a natural water content of 32%, a liquid limit of 48 and a plastic limit of 20. What is its liquidity index?
examples.idea: The liquidity index places the natural water content between the plastic limit (index 0) and the liquid limit (index 1). Values near 1 indicate a soft, sensitive soil; values near 0 or below indicate a stiff one.

examples.problem: A soil has 62% passing the No. 200 sieve, a liquid limit of 48 and a plasticity index of 22. Using GI = (F - 35)(0.2 + 0.005(LL - 40)) + 0.01(F - 15)(PI - 10), what is its AASHTO group index, rounded to the nearest whole number?
examples.idea: The AASHTO group index rates a subgrade soil within its group: the higher the number, the poorer the soil as a pavement subgrade. It is reported as a whole number in parentheses after the group symbol.

sections.deep:
Index properties classify a soil so that its behaviour can be anticipated. Grain size distribution separates gravel, sand and fines; the coefficients of uniformity and curvature describe the grading. For fine-grained soils the Atterberg limits mark the water contents at which behaviour changes, and the plasticity index is the range over which the soil is plastic.

The Unified Soil Classification System uses these results: first coarse or fine by the percentage passing the No. 200 sieve, then gravel or sand, then well or poorly graded for clean coarse soils, and the plasticity chart for fines. AASHTO classification serves highway subgrades.
method: Find the percentage passing the No. 200 sieve; more than 50% means fine-grained.
For coarse soils, decide gravel or sand from the No. 4 sieve.
With under 5% fines, compute C_{u} and C_{c} to decide well or poorly graded.
With over 12% fines, or for fine soils, use the liquid limit and plasticity index on the plasticity chart.
Write the two-letter symbol.

sections.title: Phase relations
sections.body:
Soil is three things mixed together: solid grains, water and air. Phase relations describe the mix. Void ratio is the volume of voids over the volume of solids. Porosity is the volume of voids over the total volume. Water content is the mass of water over the mass of solids. Degree of saturation is the share of the voids that is filled with water.

Draw a phase diagram, set the volume of solids to 1, and fill in the rest. Almost every question then solves itself. One identity ties everything together: Se = wG_{s}.
pitfalls: Dividing by total mass instead of dry mass for water content.

example.problem: A saturated clay has a water content of 30% and G_{s} = 2.70. Find its void ratio.

ideas.title: Start with the phase diagram
ideas.text: Sketch the three phases and fill in what is known, as you would a free-body diagram. Subtract to find the rest, and only then choose a formula. In a saturated soil there is no air, so the volume of voids equals the volume of water.

ideas.title: Density of water
ideas.text: The handbook gives the unit weight of water. For mass-based problems use 1 g/cm^{3} = 1,000 kg/m^{3}.

ideas.title: Water content
ideas.text: Water content is the mass of water divided by the mass of dry solids, so the moist mass is the dry mass times (1 + w). Dividing the moist (bulk) density by (1 + w) therefore gives the dry density.

ideas.title: Void ratio
ideas.text: Dry density relates to void ratio through the phase diagram: dry density = G_{s} × (density of water) / (1 + e). Solving for e gives the volume of voids per unit volume of solids. Do not confuse it with porosity, n = e / (1 + e).

ideas.title: Water content
ideas.text: Water content is the mass of water divided by the mass of dry solids, not by the moist mass. That is why it can exceed 100% in very soft clays and organic soils.

examples.problem: A moist soil sample has a mass of 2.10 kg and a volume of 0.001 m^{3}. Its water content is 15%. What is the dry density?
examples.idea: Water content is the mass of water divided by the mass of dry solids, so the moist mass is the dry mass times (1 + w). Dividing the moist (bulk) density by (1 + w) therefore gives the dry density.

examples.problem: A soil has a dry density of 1,700 kg/m^{3}. The specific gravity of its solids is 2.72. What is its void ratio?
examples.idea: Dry density relates to void ratio through the phase diagram: dry density = G_{s} × (density of water) / (1 + e). Solving for e gives the volume of voids per unit volume of solids. Do not confuse it with porosity, n = e / (1 + e).

examples.problem: A soil sample has a mass of 152.6 g when moist and 128.0 g after oven drying. What is its water content?
examples.idea: Water content is the mass of water divided by the mass of dry solids, not by the moist mass. That is why it can exceed 100% in very soft clays and organic soils.

examples.problem: A soil has a water content of 18%, a specific gravity of solids of 2.69 and a void ratio of 0.68. What is its degree of saturation?
examples.idea: The phase relationships link four quantities: S e = w G_{s}. The degree of saturation is the share of the void space that is filled with water.

examples.problem: A soil has a void ratio of 0.68. What is its porosity?
examples.idea: Void ratio compares the volume of voids with the volume of solids; porosity compares it with the total volume. They are linked by n = e / (1 + e), so porosity is always less than 1.

examples.problem: A fully saturated soil has a specific gravity of solids of 2.70 and a void ratio of 0.83. What is its saturated unit weight? Use 9.81 kN/m^{3} for water.
examples.idea: Take a volume of solids of 1: the solids weigh G_{s} times the unit weight of water, the water filling the voids weighs e times it, and the total volume is 1 + e.

sections.deep:
Soil is three phases: solids, water and air. The phase diagram separates them so that every weight and volume relation becomes arithmetic. Water content is weight of water over weight of solids, void ratio is volume of voids over volume of solids, porosity is volume of voids over total volume and degree of saturation is volume of water over volume of voids.

The relation S e = w G_{s} links them. Unit weights follow from the diagram: dry unit weight is G_{s} times the unit weight of water over (1 + e). Assuming a volume of solids of 1 makes most problems a matter of filling in the diagram.
method: Draw the phase diagram with volumes on the left and weights on the right.
Set the volume of solids to 1 unless a total is given.
Fill in what is known, using S e = w G_{s} to connect phases.
Read the wanted ratio from the completed diagram.
Check that saturation is between 0 and 100%.

sections.title: Laboratory and field tests
sections.body:
Tests turn a soil sample into design numbers. The Proctor compaction test finds the water content at which a soil packs densest, and that maximum dry density. Field density tests then check the contractor's compaction against it. Permeability tests measure how easily water passes: constant head for sands, falling head for clays.

Strength comes from direct shear, triaxial and unconfined compression tests. In the field, the standard penetration test counts hammer blows to drive a sampler (the N-value), and the cone penetration test pushes a cone and records resistance.
pitfalls: Comparing moist density with the Proctor dry density.

example.problem: Compacted fill has a dry density of 1,750 kg/m^{3}. The Proctor maximum is 1,850 kg/m^{3}. Does it meet a 95% specification?

ideas.title: The compaction curve
ideas.text: Too dry, and the grains lack the lubrication to pack together. Too wet, and water occupies space the grains could have filled. The peak between is the maximum dry density at the optimum water content, and more compactive effort moves the peak up and toward drier conditions.

ideas.title: Relative density is not relative compaction
ideas.text: Relative compaction is field dry density over the laboratory maximum and is what specifications state. Relative density places a granular soil between its loosest and densest states. Field density is measured with a sand cone or a nuclear gauge.

ideas.title: Relative compaction
ideas.text: Relative compaction compares the dry unit weight achieved in the field with the laboratory maximum from the Proctor test. Specifications usually require a minimum percentage, often 90% to 95%.

ideas.title: Coefficient of permeability
ideas.text: Darcy's law: flow rate = k i A, where the hydraulic gradient i is head loss divided by flow length. In a constant-head test the flow rate is the collected volume divided by time, so k = Q L / (A h t).

ideas.title: Relative density
ideas.text: Relative density places a granular soil between its loosest and densest states. In terms of dry unit weights, D_{r} = ((field - minimum) / (maximum - minimum)) × (maximum / field). It is not the same as relative compaction, which is simply field over maximum.

examples.problem: A field density test gives a dry unit weight of 17.9 kN/m^{3}. The maximum dry unit weight from the Proctor test is 18.6 kN/m^{3}. What is the relative compaction?
examples.idea: Relative compaction compares the dry unit weight achieved in the field with the laboratory maximum from the Proctor test. Specifications usually require a minimum percentage, often 90% to 95%.

examples.problem: In a constant-head permeability test, 720 cm^{3} of water passes through a sample in 300 s. The sample is 18 cm long with a cross-section of 40 cm^{2}, and the head difference is 45 cm. What is the coefficient of permeability?
examples.idea: Darcy's law: flow rate = k i A, where the hydraulic gradient i is head loss divided by flow length. In a constant-head test the flow rate is the collected volume divided by time, so k = Q L / (A h t).

examples.problem: A sand has a field dry unit weight of 16.8 kN/m^{3}. Its maximum and minimum dry unit weights are 18.4 and 14.8 kN/m^{3}. What is its relative density?
examples.idea: Relative density places a granular soil between its loosest and densest states. In terms of dry unit weights, D_{r} = ((field - minimum) / (maximum - minimum)) × (maximum / field). It is not the same as relative compaction, which is simply field over maximum.

examples.problem: In a falling-head test, a soil sample 15 cm long with a cross-section of 75 cm^{2} is fed from a standpipe of 1.2 cm^{2}. The head falls from 100 cm to 70 cm in 600 s. What is the coefficient of permeability?
examples.idea: In a falling-head test the flow comes from a narrow standpipe, so the head drops as water passes: k = (a L / (A t)) ln(h_{1} / h_{2}). It suits fine soils, where a constant-head test would pass too little water to measure.

examples.problem: A standard penetration test records 20 blows per 300 mm with a hammer that delivers 62% of the theoretical free-fall energy. What is the blow count corrected to 60% energy, N_{60}?
examples.idea: Different hammers deliver different fractions of the theoretical energy, so blow counts are normalised to a standard 60%. A more efficient hammer drives the sampler with fewer blows, and its count is scaled up.

examples.problem: A direct shear test on dry sand fails at a shear stress of 86 kPa under a normal stress of 140 kPa. Taking cohesion as zero, what is the friction angle?
examples.idea: For a cohesionless soil the failure envelope is a straight line through the origin, shear strength = normal stress × tan(friction angle). One test gives the angle directly.

sections.deep:
Laboratory and field tests supply the numbers used in design. The Proctor test finds the maximum dry density and optimum water content for compaction, and field density tests are compared with it as relative compaction. Permeability comes from constant-head tests for coarse soils and falling-head tests for fine soils.

Strength comes from direct shear, unconfined compression and triaxial tests; compressibility from the consolidation (oedometer) test. In the field, the standard penetration test gives a blow count N and the cone penetration test gives tip resistance, both correlated with density and strength.
method: Identify the test and the property it gives.
Apply the test's equation with the measured quantities.
Convert moist density to dry density by dividing by (1 + water content).
Compare field values with laboratory maxima for compaction control.
Use consistent units for permeability results.

sections.title: Effective stress
sections.body:
Total stress at a depth is the weight of everything above: soil and water. Pore water pressure is the pressure of the water in the voids. Effective stress is the difference, and it is what the soil grains actually feel. Strength and settlement depend on effective stress, not total.

Work down layer by layer. Add each layer's unit weight times its thickness for total stress. Pore pressure is the unit weight of water times the depth below the water table. Subtract. A rising water table lowers effective stress and weakens the soil.

formulas.name: Pore pressure
formulas.expr: unit weight of water × depth below water table

pitfalls: Using the saturated unit weight above the water table, or the moist one below it.

example.problem: Saturated clay (unit weight 20 kN/m^{3}) has the water table at the surface. Find the effective stress at 5 m.
example.steps:
Total = 20(5) = 100 kPa. Pore pressure = 9.81(5) = 49 kPa.

Effective stress = 51 kPa.

ideas.title: Working down a layered profile
ideas.text: Add the total stress layer by layer: unit weight times thickness, using the saturated unit weight below the water table. Pore pressure is zero above the water table and rises at 9.81 kPa per metre below it. Subtract at the depth of interest.

ideas.title: A moving water table
ideas.text: Lowering the water table raises effective stress in the soil below it, because pore pressure falls while total stress barely changes. That increase can cause settlement of compressible layers.

ideas.title: Seepage and the quick condition
ideas.text: Upward seepage reduces effective stress. At the critical hydraulic gradient, (saturated unit weight - unit weight of water) / unit weight of water, which is close to 1 for most soils, effective stress reaches zero and the soil loses its strength.

ideas.title: Effective stress
ideas.text: Effective stress is total stress minus pore water pressure. Total stress is the weight of everything above the point; pore pressure is the unit weight of water times the depth below the water table. Effective stress, not total stress, controls strength and settlement.

examples.problem: A sand deposit has a unit weight of 18.5 kN/m^{3} above the water table and a saturated unit weight of 20 kN/m^{3} below it. The water table is 2.5 m below the ground surface. What is the vertical effective stress at a depth of 7 m? Use 9.81 kN/m^{3} for water.
examples.idea: Effective stress is total stress minus pore water pressure. Total stress is the weight of everything above the point; pore pressure is the unit weight of water times the depth below the water table. Effective stress, not total stress, controls strength and settlement.
examples.steps:
Total stress = 18.5(2.5) + 20(7 - 2.5) = 136.2 kPa.

Pore pressure = 9.81(7 - 2.5) = 44.1 kPa.

Effective stress = 136.2 - 44.1 = 92.1 kPa.

examples.problem: A saturated soil with a unit weight of 19.3 kN/m^{3} lies beneath a lake. What is the vertical effective stress 6.8 m below the lake bed? Use 9.81 kN/m^{3} for water.
examples.idea: Below standing water, the weight of the water above the bed adds equally to total stress and to pore pressure, so it cancels. Effective stress is the buoyant unit weight times the depth below the bed, whatever the depth of the lake.

examples.problem: A sand has a specific gravity of solids of 2.69 and a void ratio of 0.65. What upward hydraulic gradient would cause a quick (boiling) condition?
examples.idea: Upward seepage reduces effective stress. When the seepage force equals the buoyant weight of the soil the effective stress is zero and the sand boils. That critical gradient is (G_{s} - 1) / (1 + e), usually close to 1.

examples.problem: A footing 2.0 m by 2.0 m carries a load of 950 kN. Using the 2:1 method, what is the increase in vertical stress 2.0 m below the footing?
examples.idea: The 2:1 method spreads the load outward at 2 vertical to 1 horizontal, so at depth z the loaded area has grown by z in each plan dimension. Stress increase is the load divided by that enlarged area.

sections.deep:
Soil strength and compression depend on the stress carried by the grain skeleton, the effective stress, which is the total stress minus the pore water pressure. Water in the pores carries part of the load but has no shear strength, so raising pore pressure weakens the soil even though nothing else changes.

Total stress is the weight of everything above the point. Hydrostatic pore pressure is the unit weight of water times the depth below the water table. Seepage changes the pore pressure: upward flow raises it and can reduce effective stress to zero.
method: Draw the profile with layer boundaries and the water table.
Compute total stress layer by layer.
Compute pore pressure from depth below the water table.
Subtract to get effective stress.
Recompute after any change in water level or surcharge.
sections.primer: Below the water table, water in the gaps between grains carries part of the weight above. Only the remainder, the effective stress, presses the grains together, and only that gives the soil strength.

sections.title: Stability of retaining structures
sections.body:
Soil pushes sideways on a wall. How hard depends on whether the wall moves. If it does not move, the pressure is at rest. If it yields slightly away from the soil, the pressure drops to the active value. If it is pushed into the soil, resistance rises to the passive value, which is much larger.

Rankine theory gives the coefficients from the friction angle. Lateral pressure grows linearly with depth, so the total force is a triangle acting at one third of the height. A wall is checked against sliding, overturning and bearing failure.
pitfalls: Using the passive coefficient for the soil behind a yielding wall.
Forgetting water pressure when the backfill is not drained.

example.problem: A 3 m wall retains sand with a unit weight of 17 kN/m^{3} and a friction angle of 30°. Find the active force.

ideas.title: Soil as a fluid scaled by K
ideas.text: Water presses sideways with its full vertical pressure, K = 1. Soil presses with a fraction of it: the active coefficient is well below 1 and the passive coefficient well above, which is why soil in front of an embedded toe resists strongly once the wall moves into it. The active coefficient can also be written (1 - sin(friction angle)) / (1 + sin(friction angle)).

ideas.title: Rankine
ideas.text: The Rankine active coefficient is the ratio of horizontal to vertical effective stress when the soil has expanded enough to mobilise its full strength: K_{a} = tan^{2}(45° - friction angle / 2). A stronger soil pushes less on the wall. The passive coefficient is its reciprocal.

ideas.title: Rankine
ideas.text: Active pressure grows linearly with depth, from zero at the top to K_{a} × unit weight × H at the base. The resultant is the area of that triangle, (1/2) K_{a} (unit weight) H^{2}, and it acts at one third of the height above the base.

examples.problem: A retaining wall holds back dry sand with a friction angle of 32° and a level surface. What is the Rankine active earth pressure coefficient?
examples.idea: The Rankine active coefficient is the ratio of horizontal to vertical effective stress when the soil has expanded enough to mobilise its full strength: K_{a} = tan^{2}(45° - friction angle / 2). A stronger soil pushes less on the wall. The passive coefficient is its reciprocal.

examples.problem: A 7 m high wall retains dry sand with a unit weight of 18.5 kN/m^{3}. The Rankine active coefficient is 0.307. What is the total active force per metre of wall?
examples.idea: Active pressure grows linearly with depth, from zero at the top to K_{a} × unit weight × H at the base. The resultant is the area of that triangle, (1/2) K_{a} (unit weight) H^{2}, and it acts at one third of the height above the base.
examples.steps:
Pressure at the base = 0.307(18.5)(7) = 39.8 kPa.

P_{a} = \frac{1}{2}(39.8)(7) = 139.1 kN per metre of wall, acting 2.33 m above the base.

sections.deep:
A retaining structure must resist the lateral pressure of the soil behind it. That pressure is a fraction K of the vertical effective stress. If the wall moves away from the soil the pressure drops to the active value; if it is pushed into the soil it rises to the passive value; with no movement it is at rest. Rankine theory gives K_{a} = tan^{2}(45° - friction angle / 2) and K_{p} as its reciprocal.

For uniform soil the pressure diagram is a triangle with resultant (1/2) K (unit weight) H^{2} at one third of the height. Surcharges add a rectangle and water adds its own triangle. Walls are checked for sliding, overturning and bearing.
method: Compute the earth pressure coefficient.
Draw the pressure diagram: triangle for soil, rectangle for surcharge, triangle for water.
Compute each resultant and its height above the base.
Factor of safety against sliding: resisting forces over driving forces.
Factor of safety against overturning: resisting moments over overturning moments about the toe.

sections.title: Shear strength
sections.body:
Soil fails by sliding along a surface. Its resistance to sliding is its shear strength. The Mohr-Coulomb rule says strength has two parts: cohesion, which is there regardless of load, and friction, which grows with the effective stress pressing the grains together.

Sands have friction and no cohesion. Saturated clays loaded quickly behave as if they have cohesion only, called the undrained shear strength, which is half the unconfined compressive strength.

formulas.name: Mohr-Coulomb
formulas.expr: strength = c' + (effective normal stress) tan(friction angle)

pitfalls: Using total stress instead of effective stress in the friction term.

example.problem: A dry sand with a friction angle of 32° has an effective normal stress of 150 kPa on a plane. Find its shear strength.

ideas.title: Friction angle from one test on sand
ideas.text: With no cohesion the failure envelope passes through the origin and touches the Mohr circle, so sin(friction angle) = radius / centre = (major - minor principal stress) / (major + minor principal stress).

ideas.title: Mohr-Coulomb
ideas.text: The Mohr-Coulomb criterion gives shear strength as a cohesion intercept plus a frictional part that grows with effective normal stress: strength = c' + (normal stress) tan(friction angle).

ideas.title: Unconfined
ideas.text: In an unconfined test the minor principal stress is zero and the major principal stress at failure is q_{u}. The Mohr circle therefore has a radius of q_{u} / 2, which is the undrained shear strength of a saturated clay (friction angle taken as zero).

ideas.title: Mohr-Coulomb
ideas.text: For a soil with no cohesion the failure envelope passes through the origin and is tangent to the Mohr circle at failure. The geometry gives sin(friction angle) = radius / centre = (major - minor) / (major + minor).

sections.deep:
Soil fails in shear. The Mohr-Coulomb criterion gives the shear strength on a plane as cohesion plus effective normal stress times the tangent of the friction angle. Sands have friction and little or no cohesion; saturated clays loaded quickly behave as if they had only cohesion, the undrained shear strength.

Drainage decides which strength applies. Slow loading or free-draining soil uses drained (effective stress) parameters; fast loading of clay uses undrained strength. Laboratory tests fix the parameters by plotting failure states as Mohr circles and drawing the tangent envelope.
method: Decide whether conditions are drained or undrained.
Find the effective normal stress on the failure plane.
Apply strength = c + normal stress × tan(friction angle).
For unconfined compression, undrained strength is half the compressive strength.
From triaxial data, draw the Mohr circles and read the envelope.

sections.title: Bearing capacity
sections.body:
Bearing capacity is the pressure a footing can put on the ground before the soil shears and squeezes out sideways. The ultimate value has three parts: one from cohesion, one from the weight of soil beside the footing above its base, and one from the weight of soil below it. Each is multiplied by a bearing capacity factor that depends on the friction angle.

Design uses an allowable pressure, the ultimate value divided by a factor of safety, commonly 3. Size the footing so that the column load divided by the footing area does not exceed it.
pitfalls: Dividing by the factor of safety twice, or not at all.

example.problem: A column load of 900 kN bears on soil with an allowable pressure of 200 kPa. What square footing is needed?

ideas.title: A footing with load and moment
ideas.text: A moment M on a footing shifts the resultant by e = M / P. The pressure under the two edges is (P / A)(1 ± 6e / B). If e exceeds B / 6 the lighter edge would go into tension, which soil cannot take, so that edge lifts.

ideas.title: Ultimate bearing capacity
ideas.text: Terzaghi's equation for a strip footing adds three resistances: cohesion (c N_{c}), surcharge from the soil beside the footing (unit weight × depth × N_{q}) and the weight of soil below (half × unit weight × B × N_{gamma}). For clay in undrained loading the third term is zero.

ideas.title: Bearing capacity
ideas.text: Allowable bearing pressure is the ultimate capacity divided by the factor of safety. The required area is load divided by allowable pressure, and for a square footing the width is the square root of the area.

ideas.title: Bearing capacity
ideas.text: A moment shifts the resultant by e = M / P. While e is within B / 6, the pressure under the footing is trapezoidal, with edge values (P / B)(1 ± 6e / B). The larger value is at the toe.

sections.deep:
Bearing capacity is the pressure at which the soil under a footing fails in shear. Terzaghi's equation sums three sources of resistance: cohesion, the surcharge of soil beside the footing and the weight of soil beneath it, each multiplied by a bearing capacity factor that depends on the friction angle. Shape factors adjust for square and circular footings.

Allowable bearing pressure is the ultimate value divided by a factor of safety, commonly 3. A water table near the footing reduces capacity because buoyant unit weights apply. Settlement often governs before bearing failure does.
method: Read the bearing capacity factors for the friction angle.
Compute each term: c N_{c}, surcharge × N_{q} and half × unit weight × B × N_{gamma}.
Apply shape factors for the footing type.
Divide by the factor of safety for allowable pressure.
Size the footing as load over allowable pressure.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.
sections.primer: A footing spreads a load over the ground. If the pressure is too high the soil beneath shears and the footing sinks or tilts. Bearing capacity is that limiting pressure.
terms: bearing capacity
the pressure at which the soil under a footing fails in shear
cohesion
the part of a soil's shear strength that does not depend on how hard the grains are pressed together
friction angle
the angle whose tangent is the ratio of a soil's frictional shear strength to the normal stress on it
factor of safety
resisting effect divided by driving effect; above 1 means stable
unit weight
weight per unit volume of a soil or material
moment
the turning effect of a force about a point: the force times its perpendicular distance from that point
resultant
the single force that has the same effect as several forces acting together

sections.title: Foundation types
sections.body:
Shallow foundations spread load near the surface. A spread footing carries one column, a strip footing carries a wall, and a mat carries a whole building on one slab. They suit sites where good soil is close to the surface.

Deep foundations carry load down through weak soil. Driven piles and drilled shafts resist load by friction along their sides and bearing at their tips. Choose a deep foundation when the upper soil is weak or compressible, loads are heavy, or scour could undermine a shallow footing.

formulas.name: Pile capacity
formulas.expr: Q_{ult} = (skin friction × side area) + (end bearing × tip area)

pitfalls: Using the tip area where the side (perimeter × length) area is needed.

example.problem: A 0.4 m diameter drilled shaft is 12 m long with a skin friction of 50 kPa and no end bearing. Find its capacity.

ideas.title: Shallow foundations
ideas.text: Spread footings carry single columns, combined footings carry two or more, strip footings carry walls and a mat (raft) is one thick slab under the whole structure. They suit sites where competent soil lies near the surface.

ideas.title: Deep foundations
ideas.text: Driven piles and drilled shafts carry load down to stronger material or shed it through skin friction. Use them where the upper soils are weak or compressible, loads are heavy, or uplift, lateral load or scour governs.

ideas.title: Choosing
ideas.text: A mat is chosen when individual footings would cover more than about half the plan area or when differential settlement must be limited. End-bearing piles rely on a firm stratum at the tip; friction piles rely on the shaft.
A pile carries load two ways: skin friction acting on the surface area of the shaft (perimeter × length) and end bearing acting on the tip area. The ultimate capacity is the sum.

sections.deep:
The foundation is chosen to match the structure's loads to the ground. If competent soil is near the surface, shallow foundations spread the load over enough area to keep bearing pressure and settlement acceptable. If it is not, deep foundations carry the load down to better material or shed it along their length.

Pile capacity is the sum of shaft friction and end bearing. Groups of piles may carry less than the sum of single piles. Mats tie the whole structure together and reduce differential settlement.
method: Establish the depth to competent soil and the size of the loads.
For shallow footings, size by allowable bearing pressure and check settlement.
For piles, add skin friction (unit friction × shaft surface area) and end bearing (unit resistance × tip area).
Apply the factor of safety.
Consider group effects and settlement.

sections.title: Consolidation and differential settlement
sections.body:
When clay is loaded, the water in its voids carries the load at first. The water drains slowly and the grains take over, and as they do the clay compresses and the ground settles. This is consolidation, and it can take years.

How much it settles depends on the compression index and the rise in effective stress. How long it takes depends on the square of the drainage path: with drainage at top and bottom, the path is half the layer thickness. Differential settlement, where one part of a structure sinks more than another, causes the damage.
pitfalls: Using the full layer thickness as the drainage path when the layer drains both ways.
Using natural log where log base 10 is required.

example.problem: A 2 m clay layer has C_{c} = 0.25 and e_{0} = 0.9. Effective stress rises from 80 to 160 kPa. Find the settlement.

ideas.title: Recompression, then virgin compression
ideas.text: A clay that has carried a higher stress in the past recompresses along a flat slope, C_{r}, until the stress passes its preconsolidation pressure, then follows the steep virgin slope, C_{c}. Locate the starting and final stresses against the preconsolidation pressure to choose the one-term or two-term settlement formula. Common correlations: C_{c} is about 0.009(LL - 10) and C_{r} about C_{c} / 6.

ideas.title: Compression index
ideas.text: For normally consolidated clay, void ratio falls linearly with the logarithm of effective stress, at slope C_{c}. Settlement is the change in void ratio converted to a change in layer thickness: S = C_{c} H / (1 + e_{0}) × log_{10}(final stress / initial stress).

ideas.title: Time factor
ideas.text: Consolidation time follows t = T_{v} H_{dr}^{2} / c_{v}, where H_{dr} is the longest path water must travel to drain. With drainage at both faces, H_{dr} is half the layer thickness, which makes consolidation four times faster than single drainage.

ideas.title: Compression index
ideas.text: The compression index is the slope of the virgin compression line. For undisturbed clays of low to medium sensitivity it is often estimated from the liquid limit. The recompression index is commonly taken as about one sixth of it.

examples.problem: A 8 m thick normally consolidated clay layer has a compression index of 0.32 and an initial void ratio of 0.9. The effective stress at mid-layer rises from 140 kPa to 280 kPa. What is the primary consolidation settlement?

sections.deep:
Clay settles slowly because water must drain out of its pores before the grain skeleton can compress. The amount of primary consolidation settlement comes from the compression index and the change in effective stress on a log scale; a clay that has been loaded more heavily in the past is overconsolidated and compresses much less until its preconsolidation pressure is exceeded.

The time it takes depends on the square of the drainage path and the coefficient of consolidation. Differential settlement, the difference between adjacent supports, is what damages structures.
method: Compute the initial effective stress at the middle of the clay layer.
Add the stress increase from the new load.
Apply the settlement equation for normally or overconsolidated clay.
For time, use t = T_{v} H_{dr}^{2} / c_{v}, with the drainage path halved for double drainage.
Compare settlements at adjacent footings.

compression index

effective stress

overconsolidated

normally consolidated

void ratio
volume of voids divided by volume of solid grains in a soil
liquid limit
the water content at which a clay changes from plastic to liquid behaviour

sections.title: Slope stability
sections.body:
A slope fails when the soil's strength along some surface is no longer enough to hold the weight above it. The factor of safety is resisting strength over driving force, or resisting moment over driving moment for a circular slip.

A long uniform slope in dry sand is stable as long as it is flatter than the friction angle. In clay, failure is usually along a circular arc. Water is the usual trigger: it adds weight and raises pore pressure, which cuts effective stress and strength. Flattening the slope, draining it and adding a berm at the toe all improve stability.
pitfalls: Dividing the angles themselves instead of their tangents.

example.problem: A dry sand slope with a friction angle of 33° stands at 20°. Find the factor of safety.

ideas.title: Slope failure

sections.deep:
A slope is stable when the shear strength available along any potential slip surface exceeds the shear stress that gravity produces on it. The factor of safety is the ratio of the two. For an infinite slope of dry sand it reduces to tan(friction angle) / tan(slope angle); seepage parallel to the slope roughly halves it.

Finite slopes in clay are analysed with circular slip surfaces by taking moments about the centre, and with stability charts. Water is the usual trigger of failure: it adds weight and raises pore pressure, reducing effective stress and strength.
method: Identify the slope type and soil: infinite or finite, sand or clay.
For an infinite slope, apply the ratio of tangents, adjusted for seepage if present.
For a circular slip in clay, compute resisting moment (strength × arc length × radius) over driving moment (weight × lever arm).
Compare the factor of safety with the required value, typically 1.3 to 1.5.

moment

friction angle
the angle whose tangent is the ratio of a soil's frictional shear strength to the normal stress on it
pore pressure
the pressure of the water in the spaces between soil grains
effective stress
the part of the stress in a soil that is carried by grain-to-grain contact: total stress minus pore water pressure
shear stress
force per unit area acting parallel to a surface, trying to slide one layer over the next
cohesion
the part of a soil's shear strength that does not depend on how hard the grains are pressed together

sections.title: Soil stabilization
sections.body:
Poor soil can be improved rather than replaced. Compaction is the simplest method. Chemical stabilization mixes in lime or cement: lime reacts with clay to make it less plastic and easier to work, and cement binds granular soils.

Geosynthetics are manufactured sheets and grids placed in the ground. Geotextiles separate layers, filter and drain. Geogrids reinforce. Geomembranes block water. Other methods include preloading soft clay with wick drains to speed settlement, and stone columns.

formulas.name: Additive quantity
formulas.expr: mass of additive = percent × dry mass of soil

pitfalls: Basing the additive on moist mass instead of dry mass.

example.problem: Cement at 6% by dry mass is mixed into 500 m^{3} of soil with a dry density of 1,700 kg/m^{3}. How much cement is needed?

ideas.title: Mechanical improvement
ideas.text: Compaction raises density and strength and is controlled against the Proctor maximum. Preloading with a surcharge, often with wick drains, consolidates soft clay before construction. Vibroflotation and dynamic compaction densify loose sands.

ideas.title: Chemical stabilisation
ideas.text: Lime suits plastic clays: it lowers the plasticity index and swell potential and raises strength. Portland cement suits granular and low-plasticity soils. Fly ash and bitumen are also used.

ideas.title: Geosynthetics
ideas.text: A geotextile can separate a soft subgrade from an aggregate base, filter, drain or reinforce. Geogrids reinforce. Geomembranes are barriers to water.
Stabiliser quantities are specified as a percentage of the dry mass of soil. Find the dry mass from dry density × volume, then take the percentage.

examples.problem: A clay subgrade is to be treated with 4.5% lime by dry mass. The soil has a dry density of 1,750 kg/m^{3} and 600 m^{3} is to be treated. How much lime is needed?
examples.idea: Stabiliser quantities are specified as a percentage of the dry mass of soil. Find the dry mass from dry density × volume, then take the percentage.

examples.problem: Fill is to be compacted to a dry density of 1,790 kg/m^{3}. The borrow soil arrives at a water content of 7.2% and the optimum is 12.8%. How much water must be added per cubic metre of compacted fill?
examples.idea: Water content is the mass of water divided by the mass of dry solids. The water to add is the dry mass times the increase in water content, and 1 kg of water is 1 L.
examples.steps: Water = 1,790 × \frac{12.8 - 7.2}{100} = 100.2 kg, or 100.2 L per cubic metre.

sections.deep:
Ground that is too weak, too compressible or too permeable can be improved instead of replaced. The methods either densify the soil, change its chemistry or add reinforcement. Which one works depends on the soil type: vibration densifies sands but not clays, preloading consolidates clays, and lime reacts with clay minerals while cement binds granular soils.

Compaction specifications state a minimum relative compaction and a water content range around optimum. Geosynthetics add separation, filtration, drainage or reinforcement.
